subject: Agriculture
title: India's Wheat Revolution
description: A short lesson to help you apply India's Wheat Revolution.

hook.text: In 1965, India was one bad monsoon away from mass famine. It imported 10 million tons of wheat per year.

buildup.text: India's agriculture minister, M.S. Swaminathan, brought Borlaug's dwarf wheat seeds from Mexico.

discovery.text: With new seeds, fertilizer, and irrigation, Indian wheat yields doubled in five years.

twist.text: By 1974, India was self-sufficient in wheat. It went from aid recipient to grain exporter.

climax.text: The transformation saved millions from famine but concentrated benefits in Punjab and Haryana—not everywhere.

punchline.text: New seeds turned a hungry nation into a wheat exporter in a decade.

quiz.question: Who brought Borlaug's wheat seeds to India?

details.summary: India's wheat revolution of the 1960s-70s transformed the country from a famine-threatened nation dependent on food aid into a self-sufficient wheat producer. Adoption of Borlaug's semi-dwarf varieties, combined with irrigation and fertilizer, tripled India's wheat production in just 15 years.
details.whyItMatters: India's wheat revolution is the Green Revolution's greatest success story. It averted predicted mass famine, ended dependence on U.S. food aid, and proved that developing nations could achieve food self-sufficiency through agricultural science.
takeaways: India imported 18,000 tons of Borlaug's Mexican wheat seed in 1966 amid crisis
Wheat production tripled from 12 million tons in 1965 to 47 million by 1985
India went from famine threat to wheat self-sufficiency within a single generation

faq.question: How did India adopt Green Revolution wheat varieties?
faq.answer: Indian scientist M.S. Swaminathan championed Borlaug's varieties. In 1966, India imported 18,000 tons of Mexican semi-dwarf wheat seed—the largest seed import in history. Combined with government subsidies for fertilizer and irrigation, yields doubled then tripled within two decades.

faq.question: What challenges accompanied India's wheat revolution?
faq.answer: Benefits concentrated among wealthier farmers with access to irrigation and credit. Punjab and Haryana prospered while eastern India lagged behind. Groundwater depletion, soil degradation from intensive monoculture, and rural inequality emerged as long-term consequences of the transformation.
